title: What time is it?
title_target: กี่โมงแล้ว — Kìi moong láaeo
goal: Tell the time with the Thai system that splits the day into six blocks, make appointments, and name the parts of the day — a system that looks complicated on paper but takes one sitting to learn.
bekal: ask and tell the time in the everyday Thai system
name parts of the day with ตอน
make plans: กี่โมง, เมื่อไหร่, ตอนไหน
understand the 24-hour system used at stations and airports

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — Making dinner plans
dialogs.intro: Nok and Budi are planning dinner. Notice that the same number — "six" — is used for two different times, and what tells them apart is the word that follows.

notes: **Thai splits the day into SIX blocks, and each block has its own word for the hour.** That's what makes the system look complicated, though it only needs to be learned once. The blocks: early morning (*ตี*), morning (*โมงเช้า*), noon (*เที่ยง*), afternoon (*บ่าย…โมง*), evening (*โมงเย็น*), night (*ทุ่ม*).
**The number "six" appears twice a day, and that doesn't confuse Thais** because the tails differ: *หกโมงเช้า* (6 a.m.) and *หกโมงเย็น* (6 p.m.). The words *เช้า* and *เย็น* at the end decide it.

**ทุ่ม thûm starts counting again from 7 p.m.** *หนึ่งทุ่ม* = 7 p.m., *สองทุ่ม* = 8 p.m., *สามทุ่ม* = 9 p.m., up to *ห้าทุ่ม* = 11 p.m. The word comes from the sound of the drum once beaten to mark the hours of the night.
**ตี tii counts the early-morning hours.** *ตีหนึ่ง* = 1 a.m., *ตีห้า* = 5 a.m. This also comes from the sound of a strike — *ตี* literally means "to hit".

**ครึ่ง khrûeng = half, and it goes at the end.** *หกโมงครึ่ง* = 6:30 a.m. or p.m. For other minutes, say the number and then *นาที naa-thii*: *บ่ายสองโมงยี่สิบนาที* = 2:20 p.m. In fast speech *นาที* is often dropped.

**ตอน tawn means "at the time of" and forms parts of the day.** *ตอนเช้า* (in the morning), *ตอนบ่าย* (in the afternoon), *ตอนเย็น* (in the evening), *ตอนกลางคืน* (at night), *ตอนนี้* (now). It's used far more than exact times — Thais would rather say "evening" than "five o'clock".
**อย่า yàa means "don't" and goes before the verb.** *อย่ามาสาย* = don't be late. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with *ไม่ mâi*, which only means "not"; *อย่า* is a prohibition.
**รถติด rót tìt literally means "cars stuck", and it's the word for a traffic jam.** You'll hear it every day in Bangkok, and it's an excuse for lateness that is always accepted.

grammars.title: Thai time: the whole day in one table
body: Read it once calmly, then come back whenever you need it. The last column is what people actually say.

head: Time
Block
Thai
Pronunciation
rows: เก้าโมงเช้า
สิบเอ็ดโมงเช้า
เที่ยง / เที่ยงวัน
บ่ายสองโมง
บ่ายสี่โมง
ห้าโมงเย็น

after: ⚠️ **บ่ายโมง (1 p.m.) doesn't use the number "one".** *หนึ่ง* is dropped; people say *บ่ายโมง*, not *บ่ายหนึ่งโมง*.

If all this feels like too much for today, there's a legitimate shortcut: **use the 24-hour system** — *สิบเก้านาฬิกา sìp-kâao naa-lí-kaa* (19:00). Everyone understands it; it just sounds like a station announcement. What matters is that you can **understand** the everyday system; speaking the official one won't cause anyone trouble.

after: ⚠️ *สาย sǎai* has two meanings that are easy to mix up: **late morning** and **late (not on time)**. *มาสาย maa sǎai* = to come late. They're really one idea — showing up when the morning is already well along.

blocks.title: …ดี at the end of a question
items: Adding **ดี *dii*** (good) to the end of a question turns it from an interrogation into an invitation to decide together: *กี่โมง* (what time?) versus *กี่โมงดี* (what time would be good?). Compare *กินอะไรดี* (what shall we eat?) and *ไปไหนดี* (where shall we go?).
This is one of the Thai habits that makes you sound natural fastest. It signals that you're inviting the other person to decide with you, not demanding an answer.

sections.title: Time words that often go with the clock

head: Thai
Pronunciation
English
rows: ตั้งแต่…ถึง…

blocks.text: ⚠️ **ชั่วโมง chûa-moong means "hour" as a DURATION**, while *โมง moong* marks a point in time. "Two hours" is *สองชั่วโมง*; "two o'clock" is *บ่ายสองโมง*. English makes the same distinction ("two hours" vs. "two o'clock"); Thai just uses two different words.

blocks.title: Thailand's time zone
items: Thailand uses a single time zone for the whole country: **UTC+7** — the same as Jakarta, Hanoi, and Phnom Penh, one hour behind Singapore and Hong Kong, and 12 hours ahead of New York in winter.
A useful sentence for calling home: *ที่อินโดนีเซียตอนนี้กี่โมง thîi in-doo-nii-sia tawn-níi kìi moong* — what time is it in Indonesia now? Swap in your own country's name.
